name: Kronberg's Green
lede: Kronberg's Green is a muted, olive-leaning green from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color standards, and the books we hold do not say whom it was named for.

sections.title: A name the books leave open
sections.body:
Ridgway catalogued this green in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, on plate XXXI, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 *Dictionary of Color* repeats it on plate 22, dated to 1912 [1]. Ridgway drew his roughly 4,000 named samples from many older sources, including Werner and Syme's 1821 nomenclature, his own 1886 book, the mycologist Saccardo's *Chromotaxia*, and a florists' color chart, so a name in his book is not necessarily his own coinage [2]. Who Kronberg was, and whether the name honors a person or the German town of the same name, is undocumented in the sources we hold [1][2].

It is one of several near-identical greens the ISCC-NBS system later folded in: Ridgway's plate also carried [[reed-green|Reed Green]], now treated as its nearest neighbor, and sits not far from the yellower [[baiko-brown|Baiko brown]] and the everyday [[olive]] [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Measured in LCH terms, Kronberg's Green sits at lightness 51, chroma 25, hue 108 degrees, close to [[reed-green|Reed Green]] and the darker, warmer [[yellowish-olive|Yellowish Olive]] [3]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, it appears in 1,009, about 4.2 percent, with its heaviest use in Chinese and Japanese ink paintings such as the 1501 *Bamboo and Plum* and Klimt's 1898 *After the Rain* [4]. These are computed color matches on aged, varnished paintings, never a claim about the actual pigment used [4].
